compression.title: Data Provenance Explorer
compression.lede: is the Data Provenance Initiative's explorer of its audit of AI training datasets: nearly 4,000 text, speech and video datasets, each traced to sources, creators and licences (its pages; founding paper), at the training layer of one chain whose other end is what a model credits when it answers (MMRS record).

sentences.text: The Data Provenance Explorer is the interactive explorer of the Data Provenance Initiative's audit of AI training datasets: the founding paper released "our entire audit, with an interactive UI, the Data Provenance Explorer," to trace and filter on data provenance for the most popular open-source fine-tuning collections (arXiv:2310.16787), and the MMRS record defines it as tracing "the sources and licences of AI training datasets," kinds it a database, and has practitioners follow provenance back to sources, creators and licences (MMRS record).

Its own pages introduce it as the place to "Explore the datasets included in our audit," where the DPI Explorer tool filters and analyses language-model training datasets by use case, language and more (explorer introduction; landing page), and MIT Media Lab's card, the one the composition could surface but this row could not fetch, speaks of "data explorers" built on "our extensive audits of AI data" for practitioners' decisions (MIT Media Lab, title and snippet only).

The launch post names its users: developers who "track and filter thousands of datasets for legal and ethical considerations," and scholars and journalists who explore "the composition and data lineage of popular AI datasets" (Cohere, 25 October 2023).

Its unit is the dataset, "traced to its creators, sources, licences, geographies, modalities and derivation chain" (MMRS record), as the home page has it, "Inspect dataset sources, licenses, creators, geographies, modalities, and derivation chains"; the data file the Dataset Explorer loads records those fields per dataset beside the Initiative's own licence-use, attribution and share-alike readings, 3,917 rows at this row's fetch (data_summaries.csv), and the MMRS record answers that it records attribution: "yes: sources, creators and licences per dataset" (MMRS record).

"For the first time," the launch post says, the audited datasets carry "tags to the original data sources, numerous re-licensings, creators, and other data properties" (Cohere), and the Dataset Explorer computes over any selection its text sources, generating models and the share of datasets used (Dataset Explorer).

The term is its authors': "Inconsistent tracking of the origins of a piece of data, which we refer to as data provenance, has introduced a range of legal and ethical challenges" (Longpre and Hooker, Cohere); #725 makes that tracking the second of the dimensions of provenance, "training-corpus licensing," whose object is the corpus and whose question is "Under what permissions did this data enter this system?", with the Initiative among its frameworks, beside the artifact (C2PA) and the semantic dimension, which "names the dimension that completes the C2PA ambition of trust in digital content by extending provenance from the moment of creation to the lifecycle of the meaning the content carries" (#725).

Its own count is "nearly 4,000 text, video, and speech datasets" on the Dataset Explorer, "4,000+ datasets" in "608 languages" on the home page and "4000" on the landing page, and the home page gives its source as the multimodal audit "of four thousand public text, speech, and video datasets" (ICLR 2025), with the finding that "Source content often carries stricter terms than dataset releases" (its pages).

The Capture Registry records that the composition at the name supplied this scale from the Initiative's own Dataset Explorer card while the MMRS record still gave the founding audit's 1,800, and that the record was corrected to the current scale, sourced to the card (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); the record now reads "nearly 4,000 text, video and speech datasets (the Dataset Explorer); the founding audit covered more than 1,800 text datasets" (MMRS record).

The founding paper, submitted on 25 October 2023 by Shayne Longpre, Robert Mahari, Anthony Chen, Naana Obeng-Marnu and others, convened legal and machine-learning experts "to systematically audit and trace 1800+ text datasets" with "tools and standards to trace the lineage of these datasets, from their source, creators, series of license conditions, properties, and subsequent use" (arXiv:2310.16787); the launch post of the same day counts "nearly 2,000 of the most widely used fine-tuning datasets," downloaded "tens of millions of times" (Cohere).

Researchers "from MIT, Cohere for AI, and 11 other institutions" launched it as a free platform, the audit being "the launch of a wider multi-institutional initiative, where users all over the world can contribute to the explorer" (Cohere), and the Dataset Explorer still stands under the Data Provenance Explorer with its paper and repository linked (Dataset Explorer).

Its operator, the Data Provenance Initiative (Longpre, Mahari, Chen, Obeng-Marnu and others, by the founding paper: MMRS record), calls its work "Public measurement infrastructure for AI data, model ecosystems, and real-world AI use" (its home page, which the MMRS record quotes and whose phrase the record's evidence assigns to the founding paper), and says it releases "papers, datasets, and dashboards" so that researchers, journalists, policymakers and builders can "reason from shared evidence" (home page).

#98 reads the Initiative as a project that "Documents provenance of popular AI training datasets" and states its limitation as "Documentation project, not infrastructure," and in its table of what the archive takes from others it records "Provenance schema | Data Provenance Initiative | Training-pipeline provenance | Implemented (in CHA)" (#98).

The founding audit found "license omission of 70%+ and error rates of 50%+" on widely used dataset hosting sites, "a crisis in misattribution" (arXiv:2310.16787); the MMRS record quotes the finding, #725 reports it with the further figures that "85% of licenses request attribution and 30% include share-alike clauses" and with Nature Machine Intelligence 2024 as its venue, and #1714 carries it as what "is lost before training even begins" (MMRS record; #725; #1714).

The launch post places the omission in "Crowdsourced aggregators like GitHub, Papers with Code," which miss licences for 72 to 83 percent of datasets against 30 percent under the Initiative's own protocol and list them "too permissively in up to 29 percent" of cases, so that distorted licensing "leads to cascading misattribution" (Cohere).

The audit also found "sharp divides" between commercially open and closed datasets, closed ones "monopolizing" lower-resource languages, more creative tasks, richer topic variety and newer, more synthetic data (arXiv:2310.16787), a divide the launch post calls "sharp and widening," beside "a stark Western-centric skew" in representation (Cohere).

Its second explorer, the Web Data Explorer (on the home page the Web Consent Explorer), follows "Shifting preferences in how websites allow their data to be used for AI" across 14,000 domains' terms, robots.txt and crawl restrictions (its pages), from Consent in Crisis (Longpre, Mahari, Lee and others, submitted 20 July 2024; NeurIPS 2024 on the home page, "NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks" in the MMRS record), "the first, large-scale, longitudinal audit of the consent protocols for the web domains underlying AI training corpora" (arXiv:2407.14933).

The explorer page charts HEAD-C4's "2k of the largest and most critical web domains" from 2016 to April 2024, counts a domain restricted when its robots.txt disallows the named AI crawlers, and finds "significant recent spikes in restrictions" (Web Data Explorer).

The paper finds that in 2023–2024 "~5%+ of all tokens in C4, or 28%+ of the most actively maintained, critical sources in C4" became fully restricted and that "a full 45% of C4 is now restricted" by terms of service (arXiv:2407.14933; the MMRS record quotes the second), diagnoses "ineffective web protocols," and holds, as a conditional, that "If respected or enforced, these restrictions are rapidly biasing the diversity, freshness, and scaling laws for general-purpose AI systems" (arXiv:2407.14933).

#98 reads Consent in Crisis as an "Audit of C4, RefinedWeb, Dolma" that "documents collapse of web-consent infrastructure," a "Diagnostic paper," and sets the Initiative at "L4: Provenance / Consent," where what is missing is "Integrated provenance in training pipeline" (#98).

Its authors state that "major legal ambiguities remain in data licensing that the authors acknowledge cannot be resolved by tooling alone" (Cohere), and #725 states the dimension's own bound: "The Data Provenance Initiative audits whether datasets were licensed, not whether synthesized outputs preserve attribution to the human sources whose labor the synthesis depended upon"; "Licensing audits operate on the *input* to AI systems. They do not address the *output*," and the Initiative's 70%+ omission "establishes the licensing dimension's urgency; semantic provenance addresses the dimension that follows" (#725).

The dimensions are independent, "a licensed dataset can produce outputs with excellent semantic provenance if the synthesis preserves attribution; an unlicensed dataset can produce outputs that nonetheless cite their sources clearly," and the frameworks that address "the corpus," the Initiative among them, "are not designed to address the survival of authorial lineage through AI synthesis" (#725).

"The Data Provenance Initiative tells you whether the dataset was licensed," and none of these instruments was designed to tell "what happened to the meaning … between the dataset and the answer" (#725); #1003 groups "C2PA, the Data Provenance Initiative, W3C PROV" as studies that "have focused on attribution loss in AI outputs" (#1003).

The MMRS record sets the Explorer at one end of a chain: "It records provenance at the training layer, where the census's reception aggregators record it at the composition layer. The two ends of one chain: what a model was given, and what it credits when it answers" (MMRS record), with its roles provenance and monitoring (MMRS record); the Initiative's own four systems "trace AI from source data and web consent to model markets and real-world use" (home page).

At the answering end, PER "applies to these only indirectly" where claims are parametric, and reaching them at the substrate level "requires companion infrastructure (training-data provenance records, watermarking, content credentials)" (#95); #623 counts standardized documentation of training-data provenance as "a step toward the accounting the framework demands" (#623).

#1714 states the requirement across the chain, "Provenance has to survive the training pipeline," since neither audit nor influence tracing "recovers authorship" and "what survives depends on what is recorded and computed," so that sources can be "recorded at ingestion, the record kept with the training set" (#1714), where the founding audit traced lineage as far as a dataset's "subsequent use" (arXiv:2310.16787).

The MMRS record keeps each assertion with "a source and a basis" and keeps lifecycle (active, observed 2026-10-28) apart from the observation that saw it, and it states its own limits: it has not read "the explorers' pages directly (they render by script)" and takes the Initiative's page text from "the Overview's cards" (MMRS record).

The Initiative lists coverage by "the Financial Times, The New York Times, The Washington Post, MIT Technology Review, IEEE Spectrum, and VentureBeat" and use in "public AI safety and governance reporting" (home page), and at "data provenance explorer" Google's AI Overview said what the explorer is and what can be filtered in it "from the Initiative's own pages," reaching pages the record's fetcher could not render (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), the capture standing in the record as "the composition layer's account of the entity" (MMRS record).

The Capture Registry finds that "The audits that make the explorer a provenance instrument are left out": "The founding audit's licence findings and Consent in Crisis are not given; the consent explorer stands for the second" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The composition named the Initiative and cited its pages, with Shayne Longpre and Sara Hooker on the Cohere card only, and no card cited the MMRS record, which had landed the same night (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29, checked against the record and the entity's own pages); Wikipedia has no article for "Data Provenance Explorer" or "Data Provenance Initiative," and its search finds neither phrase in any article (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

D725-08.quote: Licensing audits operate on the *input* to AI systems. They do not address the *output*. A model trained on properly licensed scholarship can still produce outputs that erase the scholarship's lineage. Licensing provenance and semantic provenance are different problems requiring different instruments. The DPI's documentation of 70%+ license-omission rates establishes the licensing dimension's urgency; semantic provenance addresses the dimension that follows.
D725-08.source_label: #725 Provenance After AI Metadata Packet for Disambiguation: From Artifact Authenticity to Licensing Audit to Semantic Provenance

O725-06.quote: The dimensions are independent: a C2PA-signed image can carry meaning whose lineage has been eroded; a licensed dataset can produce outputs with excellent semantic provenance if the synthesis preserves attribution; an unlicensed dataset can produce outputs that nonetheless cite their sources clearly. Solving any one dimension does not solve the others.
O725-06.source_label: #725 Provenance After AI Metadata Packet for Disambiguation: From Artifact Authenticity to Licensing Audit to Semantic Provenance

D725-01.quote: Existing provenance frameworks address the artifact (C2PA / Content Credentials) and the corpus (Data Provenance Initiative, EU AI Act transparency provisions, W3C PROV). They are not designed to address the survival of authorial lineage through AI synthesis.
D725-01.source_label: #725 Provenance After AI Metadata Packet for Disambiguation: From Artifact Authenticity to Licensing Audit to Semantic Provenance

D725-09.quote: The Data Provenance Initiative tells you whether the dataset was licensed. EU AI Act transparency provisions tell you whether the content was AI-generated. None of these instruments was designed to tell you what happened to the meaning between the camera and the screen, between the dataset and the answer, between the source and the synthesis.
D725-09.source_label: #725 Provenance After AI Metadata Packet for Disambiguation: From Artifact Authenticity to Licensing Audit to Semantic Provenance
